Déontologie policière : une réforme qui: Police Ethics: A Reform That Favours the Police Lobby at the Expense of Victims’ Families?
Pour la famille Kalubi, le chemin qui mè: For the Kalubi family, the road to healing hearts and minds looks long.
Mbombo Tshiteya et Quelyna Kalubi, la mè: Mbombo Tshiteya and Quelyna Kalubi, David Kalubi’s mother and sister.
David Tshiteya Kalubi est décédé à l’âge: David Tshiteya Kalubi died at the age of 23 in a holding cell at the Palais de justice de Montréal on November 8, 2017. He was waiting to appear before a judge after being arrested the day before on two outstanding warrants. David’s death led to a police ethics hearing. Officers Dominique Gagné and Mathieu Paré of the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) <l1>were summoned to appear</l1> before the Police Ethics Committee following the young man’s death. The hearings, which began almost five years after David died, were held in October 2022. Surrounded by family members and her children, Mbombo Tshiteya did not miss a single hearing, at times making her displeasure or disapproval known during the officers’ testimony. Now and then she could be seen shrugging her shoulders or shaking her head, murmuring things like “But that’s not true!” or “They (the police officers) are not telling the truth,” and more. On the second day of the hearing, her son Jonathan, David’s older brother, let his frustration out aloud, prompting administrative judge Benoit McMahon to step in. While saying he understood the family members’ pain, he asked them to stay calm so the hearings could proceed without a hitch.
Les six jours de procès, au cours desque: The six days of hearings, during which investigators from the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes (BEI) and the SPVM officers mentioned above took the stand in turn, ended with the officers being found guilty. Judge McMahon ruled that Mathieu Paré and Dominique Gagné had violated sections 5, 7, 8 and 10 of the Code of Ethics of Quebec Police Officers by submitting a “statement they knew to be false or inaccurate” and by showing “negligence and recklessness with regard to the health and safety of Mr. Kalubi, who was in their care.”
Pour la famille Tshiteya, le procès a ét: For the Tshiteya family, the hearing was both a moment of relief and a form of therapy. It was in the hearing room that Mbombo Tshiteya and her family learned, for the first time, the facts and details surrounding David’s death. To put it plainly, it took five long years for this family of Congolese origin to get a clear idea of the circumstances of this tragic death. “Before these hearings, we were completely in the dark,” Mbombo Tshiteya told me on the second day of the hearings, as we stood in the lobby of 500 René-Lévesque Ouest, the building that houses the Police Ethics Committee.
Devoir vivre la mort de son enfant reste: Having to live through the death of one’s child is without a doubt the worst ordeal a parent can endure. I saw this in talking with Mbombo Tshiteya, David Tshiteya Kalubi’s mother. The years go by, but the pain and the memories remain vivid. “It’s really strange! As soon as we get close to the date of David’s death, memories come back to the surface. It’s like that every year in November and December,” she tells me. “It wakes up; you feel the pain in the same place; you remember things and you ask yourself questions in everything you do; you don’t feel like doing anything. It’s like post-traumatic aftereffects. We live with it, we’re used to it, but as soon as that period approaches, it’s as if we were sick.”
Mbombo Tshiteya m’explique que toute la: Mbombo Tshiteya explains to me that the whole family remains marked by David’s death. Every year, her son Jonathan reminds her of the fateful moment when he learned the sad news. “Mom, do you remember, it was at this hour that they came knocking on the door to announce David’s death,” she recounts. Jonathan was the first to learn of his brother’s death.
Une épreuve difficile pour les Tshiteya,: A difficult ordeal for the Tshiteyas, on top of other twists and turns the family now has to deal with.
En effet, cette année, l’anniversaire de: Indeed, this year the anniversary of David’s death comes in a particular context. On one hand, the SPVM officers cited in this case have decided to appeal their conviction. On the other, last October the Quebec National Assembly passed a bill that eliminates the right of third parties to file police ethics complaints. Yet it was precisely thanks to a complaint filed by a third party, activist Alexandre Popovic, spokesperson for the Coalition Against Police Repression and Abuse (CRAP), that the officers involved in David Kalubi Tshiteya’s death were summoned to appear in police ethics proceedings.
Pour la famille Kalubi, qui pensait avoi: For the Kalubi family, who thought they had turned the page on this painful saga, the road to healing hearts and minds looks long. The immense grief of having lost a son and a brother is compounded by anger and incomprehension in the face of a situation they would have gladly done without. “I find it outrageous, especially when you know that we lost a child and that these police officers hid the truth,” Mbombo Tshiteya fumes, for whom this situation “awakens painful memories.”
La mère de David se l’explique d’autant: David’s mother finds it all the harder to understand given that the officers were sentenced to 22 days’ suspension without pay. A “slap on the wrist,” she says.
Elle souligne que, depuis la mort de son: She points out that since her son’s death, her family and she have had to cope with a difficult situation, feeling they were not treated by the authorities as they should have been. “They treated us like a number. There was a will to prove that it wasn’t criminal. The file moved along like that, and then it was closed,” she remembers.
Le Directeur des poursuites criminelles: The Director of Criminal and Penal Prosecutions (DPCP) had indeed concluded that the evidence on file did not support a finding that officers Mathieu Paré and Dominique Gagné had shown criminal negligence.
Pour la famille Tshiteya, c’est la décep: For the Tshiteya family, it was a disappointment, especially as they were left to fend for themselves throughout the investigation, says David Kalubi’s mother. “We were presented with a fait accompli. They said the officers were not criminally responsible, and that was it,” she says.
M<sup>me</sup> Tshiteya affirme que le B: M<sup>s</sup>. Tshiteya says the BEI never told her that the officers had made false statements in the case involving her son. At the time of writing, the BEI had not responded to La Converse’s requests on this matter.
En plus d’avoir l’impression d’avoir été: Besides feeling abandoned, the Tshiteya family had to deal with press articles that seemed to dwell on “things that were not appropriate,” says Mbombo Tshiteya. Notably, the fact that David was known to police or used psychoactive substances. “They even insinuated that he died of an overdose,” she says bitterly.
La famille Tshiteya reste persuadée que: The Tshiteya family remains convinced that the circumstances surrounding David Kalubi’s death have not been fully clarified.
Du décès du jeune homme aux conclusions: From the young man’s death to the DPCP’s conclusions, including the coroner’s, the Tshiteya family felt they remained completely in the dark. In fact, it was through La Converse that they learned that the officers involved in David’s death had been summoned to appear before the Police Ethics Committee following a complaint filed by Alexandre Popovic.
Ce fut à la fois un choc et une surprise: It was both a shock and a surprise for the Tshiteyas. David’s mother remembers: “I’m a believer. I had told myself I had no tools to face what we were going through. I wondered what I should do. Should I talk to God? Should I take some kind of action? When would we get an answer? That was the subject of my prayers. And when we heard about Popovic, I told myself: ‘There it is! God heard our prayers.’”
Alexandre Popovic est arrivé dans le dos: Alexandre Popovic came into the case, and into the Tshiteyas’ lives, by chance. He learned of the matter while reading an article in the Journal de Montréal. “I saw a newspaper article that mentioned a young man barely 23 years old had died in detention, while waiting to appear in municipal court over a minor matter,” recalls the CRAP spokesperson. “Without really knowing many other details, I told myself this story didn’t smell right.”
Les policiers ont une obligation déontol: Police officers have an ethical duty toward a person held in their custody. They must look after that person’s health and safety. David Kalubi’s death therefore intrigued Alexandre Popovic, who is deeply involved in cases related to problematic police conduct. “I told myself something hadn’t worked in the system,” he explains. In the following days, he decided to file a complaint against officers Mathieu Paré and Dominique Gagné, knowing that a BEI investigation was then under way. “I figured two investigations were better than one. By filing a complaint, I knew it would trigger a police ethics investigation, given that it involved a death,” he says.
Des plaintes contre la police ou des pol: Alexandre Popovic has filed dozens and dozens of complaints against the police or individual officers, to the point of being considered one of the most prolific complainants in Quebec’s police ethics system. While most of them were rejected, as he himself confided to me, the one concerning officers Paré and Gagné went all the way, resulting in the officers being summoned before the Ethics Committee.
Pour Alexandre Popovic, l’étonnement le: For Alexandre Popovic, astonishment vies with satisfaction, especially as complaints against police officers very rarely reach this stage of the process. “It was in October-November 2020. I learned that the Police Ethics Commissioner had filed a citation before the Committee against Mathieu Paré and Dominique Gagné,” Popovic recalls. “Like I said, I’ve filed a lot of complaints, and I haven’t had many results like that. So yes, for me, that alone is a victory.”
La suite, c’est une audience d’une semai: What followed was a week-long hearing before the Ethics Committee. Present at the hearings, I was able to observe the attention with which Alexandre Popovic followed the case. Pen and small notebook in hand, with members of the Tshiteya family seated beside him, he took notes the way a journalist covers a matter of public interest. He can boast of having succeeded in getting two SPVM officers summoned before the Ethics Committee, to the point of having them found guilty of breaches of police ethics, but his room to manoeuvre is now reduced, given the new provisions of Bill 14 on public safety, assented to last October.
<strong>Une disposition de la loi qui hé: A Provision of the Law That Raises Hackles
L’ancienne loi prévoyait que n’importe q: The old law provided that anyone could file a police ethics complaint. The new one, tabled by Public Security Minister François Bonnardel, limits that right to people present at the scene of a police intervention as parties or witnesses, as well as people who are victims of police misconduct.
Le député de Québec solidaire André Font: Québec solidaire MNA André Fontecilla, who had argued for keeping the old system during the study of the bill, is worried. He believes the new version of the law will create more problems than it solves. “With the current law, we have just seriously restricted the public’s ability to obtain justice in cases of deviation, of breaches of the Police Code of Ethics,” he says.
Pour Alexandre Popovic, c’est un recul i: For Alexandre Popovic, it is a major step backward for people like him who campaign against reprehensible police behaviour. “With this law, I expect to lose the right to file complaints as I did in other cases,” he laments, before adding: “If I come across a newspaper article, for example, and realize something is wrong, I won’t be able to do what I was able to do in David Kalubi’s case.”
Un avis que partage Lynda Khelil, respon: Lynda Khelil, mobilization coordinator at the Ligue des droits et libertés, shares that view. “With the new law, if a similar situation (to David Kalubi’s) occurs, the officers might not be the subject of a police ethics complaint and might not be summoned to appear,” she notes.
Si les plaignants tiers ne peuvent plus: While third-party complainants can no longer file complaints on behalf of others, the new law nevertheless provides a reporting mechanism allowing anyone to bring to the Commissioner’s attention “the conduct of a police officer in the performance of their duties that may constitute a breach of the Code of Ethics.”
Le problème ici, insiste Popovic, c’est: The problem here, Popovic insists, is that third-party complainants like him will no longer enjoy the privileges granted to complainants, such as the right to follow the course of an investigation, to be informed of the reasons a complaint was dismissed, or even to request a review of a decision before another body of the Police Ethics Committee. The Committee’s obligation to be accountable becomes optional with the reporting mechanism. “So, less transparency,” Popovic observes.
Quid des interventions policières problé: What about problematic police interventions where there is no witness to file a complaint? What room do family members who did not witness a police intervention involving one of their own have?
Lynda Khelil et Virginie Lemire affirmen: Lynda Khelil and Virginie Lemire say their room to manoeuvre is limited. Unless they are direct witnesses to a police intervention, they must essentially make do with the reporting mechanism. And even where there is a witness, it is not certain that person will file a police ethics complaint if they are unaware of the complaint process. “There are also many people who have no trust in the police ethics system,” Lynda Khelil points out. “In fact, when we talk about the ethics system, we often hear people say: ‘What’s the point?’, ‘It’s pointless!’, ‘It’s a complaint-rejecting machine!’”
Virginie Lemire ne dit pas autre chose,: Virginie Lemire says much the same, having often handled cases involving police officers. She has observed a phenomenon of self-censorship among witnesses, especially if they are facing criminal charges following a police intervention. “People who are charged, for example, with obstruction and other offences during a police intervention don’t want to file complaints against officers who may testify at their criminal trial until they are acquitted,” the lawyer explains. “And the time limit for police ethics is even shorter; it’s one year, which is excessively short.”
La proportion de plaintes de plaignants: Since the proportion of third-party complaints that make it before the Police Ethics Committee is significant, as we will see below, the lawyer suggests looking into the reasons that lead direct witnesses not to file complaints.
Dans ces circonstances, le rôle des pers: In these circumstances, the role of people with no direct connection to the police intervention proves important. Lynda Khelil and Virginie Lemire insist that third-party complainants help shed light on situations and events that otherwise would never have been brought to the Police Ethics Commissioner’s attention. They make it possible to file a complaint when the victim cannot or does not want to. “By preventing a third party who was not present during a police intervention from filing a complaint, we deprive ourselves of the complaint process for an event in which there was a death, a serious injury or a violation of rights,” Lynda Khelil concludes.
La plupart des personnes interviewées da: Most of the people interviewed for this article are not convinced by the Commissioner’s arguments. Wary, Virginie Lemire is waiting to see how things play out on the ground. According to the lawyer, “police officers have extraordinary powers in society; we need a strong body, one capable of ensuring reflection on police work and ensuring accountability for officers who commit wrongs that go beyond the limits.” She believes that with the new law, “we are going in a completely different direction.”
De son côté, André Fontecilla estime lui: For his part, André Fontecilla also believes the new system “undermines at its foundation the ethics system that was originally set up to give the public greater confidence in the conduct of members of police forces.” The reporting mechanism, Virginie Lemire points out, does not offer sufficient guarantees in terms of accountability and transparency because of the total discretion surrounding the handling of reports. “If they refuse to act on a complaint, they don’t have to give reasons and there is no right of review.” She believes that “we are heading toward an opaque system.”
Elle prône le libre choix, autrement dit: She advocates free choice, in other words a return to the old system, which allowed anyone to go to the Police Ethics Commissioner to file a complaint over a police officer’s problematic conduct in the performance of their duties. The reporting system should not come at the expense of third-party witnesses. “People must be given the choice,” she insists. “Someone who is able to support a case and put it together properly, as is clearly the case for a number of third-party complaints that resulted in sanctions before the Committee, does not deserve to have that right taken away.”
La juriste en veut pour preuve une <l1>é: As proof, the lawyer points to a <l1>study by the Université de Montréal</l1> that compares complaints submitted to the Commissioner by third-party witnesses with those made by direct witnesses or people directly involved in events involving police officers.
Selon cette étude, les plaintes déposées: According to this study, complaints filed by third-party complainants made up 3.2% of all complaints received by the Police Ethics Commissioner from 2015 to 2020. Despite being a tiny minority, these complaints “are the ones that went the furthest in the ethics process,” the study’s authors write. Their share is significant, since they accounted for 22.6% of the complaints that led to a decision by the Police Ethics Committee, and 27.9% of those that led to sanctions. Proof that “the old system worked,” says Virginie Lemire, who still doesn’t understand why it was abolished. “How can we keep trusting our institutions if they make this kind of decision, which isn’t supported by the numbers at all?” she asks.
Alexandre Popovic reste persuadé que le: Alexandre Popovic remains convinced that the police force comes out of the legislative change that was just carried out stronger than before. “It’s a major victory for the police lobby, which has been fighting for years to weaken a police ethics system that is already weak, that is already underfunded,” he laments.
Un argument que j’ai entendu lors de mes: It’s an argument I heard in my interviews with some members of civil society, and it doesn’t seem to be without merit. Indeed, in a brief submitted in 2020 as part of the consultations on policing in Quebec, the Police Ethics Commissioner notes that complaints from third-party complainants have generated “an enormous amount of controversy among police services and the associations representing police officers’ interests.” The Commissioner points out that many believe this situation “discredits the police ethics system.”
Tout en reconnaissant la nécessité de co: While acknowledging the need to preserve the ability of an uninvolved citizen to report a situation they consider problematic, and also acknowledging that “these complaints are useful to the Commissioner’s mission since the Commissioner cannot act on their own initiative,” the Commissioner wanted to propose “a new model that would address the concerns expressed” by police forces.
Selon Lynda Khelil, la nouvelle loi est: According to Lynda Khelil, the new law is a response by Public Security Minister François Bonnardel to requests made by the then Police Ethics Commissioner, Marc-André Dowd, and by the advisory committee on policing, which also took up the Commissioner’s recommendations, as well as to those of police forces and the associations that represent their interests.
Mbombo Tshiteya, elle, reste persuadée q: Mbombo Tshiteya, for her part, remains convinced that her experience proves the old system worked well. Her gestures determined, her eyes worried, she says she is “disappointed” by the new law and believes it “should never have been adopted.” She wonders: “Mr. Popovic came to the aid of people like us, who were wronged and who had a loved one torn away from us, and I wonder how such a law can be passed. Are they trying to protect crooked cops?”
Au moment d’écrire ces lignes, le bureau: At the time of writing, François Bonnardel’s office had still not responded to La Converse’s requests.
Contactée par La Converse, M<sup>e</sup>: Reached by La Converse, M<sup>e</sup> Mélanie Hillinger, the Police Ethics Commissioner, says she no longer has the power to comment on Bill 14, which came into force on October 5, only to enforce it. However, her spokesperson, M<sup>e</sup> Michelle-Audrey Avoine, wanted to clarify some of the changes brought about by the new law. “The objective of both a complaint and a report is the same, namely to allow any person to bring a situation to the Commissioner’s attention,” she explains, before adding: “A complaint or a report will be handled with the same rigour, under the same analytical framework and in keeping with the same organizational values (...).” According to M<sup>e</sup> Michelle-Audrey Avoine, only the follow-up with the person who filed the report may differ, since that person will not have been present at the scene of the event, and out of a concern to preserve the confidentiality of sensitive information.
Par ailleurs, le plaignant tiers aura dr: Furthermore, third-party complainants will be entitled to the same information as direct complainants, with the exception of sensitive information that could concern the police officer involved or the person involved in the event, or that would reveal police intervention tactics. According to M<sup>e</sup> Avoine, “this is not about taking away rights because a person’s status changes (filing a report rather than a complaint), but rather about protecting information that is not a matter of public record.”
Un argument que relativise M<sup>e</sup>: It’s an argument that M<sup>e</sup> Virginie Lemire, a lawyer involved in police cases, puts into perspective. According to her, privacy protection should not be a pretext to justify just anything. “If there really are people who feel their privacy is being violated by this system, we need to talk about it, it needs to be demonstrated and examples need to be given,” she stresses.
Au sujet des familles des personnes impl: Regarding the families of people involved in a problematic police intervention, M<sup>e</sup> Avoine points out that “it will be possible to provide for special procedures to handle a report filed by a family member of a person who was involved in a police intervention.” She adds: “Indeed, the Commissioner is aware that this person’s sensitivity to the events is different from that of a person who is a complete stranger to them.”
M<sup>e</sup> Avoine a toutefois tenu à: M<sup>e</sup> Avoine nonetheless sought to put things in perspective. She explains these changes by citing, among other things, the need to meet complaint processing deadlines. “In recent years, certain circumstances have caused delays in processing complaints and thus increased the pressure on the Commissioner’s team,” she explains, before adding: “The discussions held as part of the consultations on the realities of policing took these factors into account, and the resulting proposals sought to strike the best balance between fulfilling the mission and making judicious use of available resources.”
